headlines.title: Ex-Google recruiter: You're answering 'Tell me about yourself?' all wrong, and other job interview mistakes—do this instead
headlines.summary: Former Google recruiter Farah Sharghi shares her best advice for how to turn coffee chats into real introductions and interviews.
headlines.article_text: Ex-Google recruiter how to avoid 3 common job interview mistakes Skip Navigation Related Stories Work Ex-Google recruiter: Why this common mistake makes your resume 'invisible' Work 3 signs work is consuming your life—and what to do about it: ‘Catch it now,' says expert Raising Successful Kids Harvard- and Stanford-trained child psychiatrist: 5 habits of parents who raise highly resilient kids Psychology and Relationships 5 ways to be more yourself and stop worrying if you're ‘good enough’ Work Use this 4-word phrase to stand out after a job interview: 'It can be really powerful,' says career coach Solstock | E+ | Getty Images In a job market that can seem impossible to break into, relationships still matter and are often what will get your foot in the door. But if your coffee chats and informational interviews keep ending with "Let's stay in touch," and then nothing happens, you might be wondering where you went wrong. I've spent more than a decade recruiting for companies like Google, TikTok, Uber and The New York Times. I've found that when people try to network, one of the biggest things that trips them up is the seemingly simple question: "Tell me about yourself?" It can unlock referrals, more introductions and interviews — but only if you know how to answer it. When someone recommends you for a role at their company, they are often asked to fill out a form where they write how they know you and why you'd be good at the job. That note is where your coffee chat either turns into an interview or goes nowhere. So the next time you are meeting with someone who does the work you want to do, or is employed at your dream company, remember that you're not there to impress them. You want to help them answer the question they will be asked afterward, which is "Why should we talk to this person?" Here's my best advice for how to navigate three of the most common job interview mistakes. Answer 'Tell me about yourself?' in 30 words or less When they hear "So, tell me about yourself," most people answer with a list of their accomplishments. The problem with that is that it gives your potential referrer nothing to hold on to. That's the wrong approach. Instead, break down the answer into three parts. Who are you now? One simple line. "I'm a supply chain analyst." What is the career move you're trying to make? Be specific. "Interested in moving into strategy" tells them something about your actionable goals. "Looking for growth" is vague and doesn't give them anything to work with. Why did you reach out to them? You wanted to talk to this person for a reason. Cogently explain why. They likely made the career move you want, or they're in the role you're aiming for. This is how it should sound when you combine them: "I'm a supply chain analyst. I reached out because you moved from operations into strategy and that's exactly what I would like to do." That's under 30 words and it gives your informational interviewer a clear place to start when they recommend you. "Supply chain analyst moving from operations into strategy" is the first line of your referral note, and you just wrote it for them. You want to avoid this this 'typical' question You've cleared that first hurdle, but the next mistake people often make is that they will ask: "What is a typical day for you?" This will only get you a vague, unhelpful description of their responsibilities. A stronger question is: "What part of your job do you find to be the most rewarding?" When you ask this, they have to think about a specific moment, instead of a general list. This way you will find out what the job feels like on a good day, which the job description will never tell you. Follow that up with "How is your performance measured at the end of the year?" When a hiring manager opens a new role, in my experience, one of the first things the recruiter asks them is, "What does success look like in the first 30 days and in the first 90 days?" But almost none of that makes it into the job description either. With this approach, you get specific and quantified details that will help you better frame your expertise in an interview setting. Invite your conversation partner to tell you a story You're almost there, but now another trap is waiting for you. You're talking with someone you admire and whose expertise you value, so an understandable question is: "What advice would you give to someone who is just starting out?" Please don't do this. It will generally only yield a response like "work hard" or "be curious." To get the information that will actually help you in the next phase of your job hunt, ask these questions instead: "When you think about a recent new hire you enjoyed working with, what qualities come to mind?" When you ask about one person who did well, that means they have to give you specifics. Then with those details, you can share a related anecdote about how you have demonstrated those traits in your previous work. "What has surprised you most about your role?" You can also ask "What do you wish you'd known before you took the job?" Surprise doesn't necessarily connote a negative experience, but this question is a great way to subtly find out where the pitfalls and unexpected stressors are. Even if you are trying to suss out what someone doesn't like about their job, phrasing it this way won't set off any alarm bells for people who won't ever complain about their employer. "What's happening in the industry right now that you think more people should know about?" You hear their view, you get to share yours and demonstrate that you've done your homework. And you can use what they tell you in your next real interview. Before your meeting ends, make sure to ask "Based on what we discussed today, is there anyone else you think I should talk to?" It's important to highlight the discussion part first. Without it, you're asking them to go through everyone they know and pick someone at random. They'll probably say "Let me think about it." But with the first part, you've narrowed it down for them. The worst they can say is "Sorry, I can't think of anyone," and that's fine. But ask every time. That's how one coffee chat can lead to introductions, referrals and interviews. Farah Sharghi is a technical recruiter, career coach and public speaker. She has worked as a talent acquisition specialist for Google, Lyft, Uber, TikTok and The New York Times. In addition to her work as a recruiter and career advisor, she is also a content creator whose posts on job hunting, interview prep and salary negotiations can be viewed on YouTube , Instagram , LinkedIn and TikTok . headlines.article_text: Anthropic sets price range of $70 to $78 in upcoming IPO Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share. Should the offering take place in mid-November as expected, it will come roughly five months after SpaceX's record IPO. Anthropic has filed to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT." In this article ANT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:35 06:35 Anthropic sets price range of $70 to $78 in upcoming IPO Squawk Box Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share, according to an updated filing on Tuesday, bringing the 5-year-old artificial intelligence lab a step closer to a potentially historic Nasdaq debut. The company is planning to price on Nov. 18 and trade on Nov. 19, according to people familiar with the details who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is targeting retail allocation of about 20%, the people said, a much higher percentage than the typical initial public offering, which is 5% to 10% for retail investors. At the high end of the range, Anthropic would net up to $64.35 billion in proceeds through the IPO. The company could end up being worth up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis, rising from the $965 billion valuation it announced as part of a funding round in May. Read more CNBC news on Anthropic PRO: Anthropic is about to go public. Here are the proxies that could benefit Anthropic releases Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 ahead of IPO Anthropic reports $17 billion in Q3 revenue, purchase commitments of $895.4 billion in revised S-1 Anthropic said it has entered into an agreement with Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. to purchase $26 billion of the company's Class N common stock in a private placement at a price per share equal to the IPO price. The shares sold in the private placement will not be registered in the offering and will not be subject to lock-up agreements with the underwriters, the company said. As Anthropic executives get set to pitch the offering to investors, they have to contend with a tumultuous political environment , following last week's midterm elections that included a Democratic sweep in Congress and the passage of numerous statewide ballot measures that could slow the AI buildout. They're also facing a public market that's grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade on concern that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for companies that need it for costly infrastructure purchases. CNBC reported last week that some Anthropic investors were bracing for a lower valuation than had previously been expected. While Anthropic had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation until recently, shareholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a "stretch." Should Anthropic reach the Nasdaq this month as planned, under the ticker symbol "ANT," the debut would come roughly five months after SpaceX went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. Elon Musk's reusable rocket and AI company has a market cap of just under $2 trillion, around its valuation at the time of the IPO. Institutional demand for Anthropic is even stronger than it was for SpaceX at this point in the process, the people said. The company's book is already covered at the $70 to $78 per share range on an allocable basis, they said. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the AI lab in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and the company primarily sells its products and services to other businesses. On Monday, Anthropic introduced two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the first time the company has released so-called frontier models since Amodei called to slow down the pace of AI development in September . Anthropic said that the models went through rigorous safety and alignment testing, and that the company developed new evaluations and post-launch monitoring tools ahead of the release. For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said. Anthropic said in its amended filing Tuesday that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month. "Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort. We hope you will share our ambition to see it though." headlines.title: Rivian CEO says new R2 SUV, autonomy make 2027 an ‘inflection year’ as EV maker marks five years since IPO
headlines.summary: Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe says 2027 will be an “inflection year” as the EV maker scales R2 and invests in autonomy.
headlines.article_text: Rivian CEO: 2027 will be an ‘inflection year’ as R2, autonomy ramp up Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Five years after Rivian shares began trading on the Nasdaq, CEO RJ Scaringe told CNBC he's betting that R2 and autonomy can make 2027 an "inflection year" for the EV maker. R2 became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle in the third quarter, and the company plans a limited point-to-point rollout of its advanced driver-assistance system before a broader release in 2027. Rivian's stock price is down more than 80% since the Amazon-backed company debuted at $78 per share five years ago, including a nearly 30% decline this year. In this article RIVN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT RJ Scaringe and team on opening day at Rivian's manufacturing campus in Normal, IL. Source: Rivian It's been five years since Rivian Automotive celebrated its initial public offering with CEO and founder RJ Scaringe ringing the Nasdaq opening bell from the company's factory in Normal, Illinois, while the company's sleek vehicles sat outside the stock exchange in Times Square. It was a euphoric time for all-electric vehicle companies that has since diminished . And much like the EV hype, Rivian's stock price is down more than 80% since the Amazon -backed company debuted on the Nasdaq at $78 per share on Nov. 10, 2021. That includes a nearly 30% decline this year. A host of internal and external factors have contributed to Rivian's stock decline, but the company continues to be the most promising EV maker to emerge during the early 2020s, as most of its peer group to go public during that time no longer exists . watch now VIDEO 9:03 09:03 Rivian CEO on five-year IPO anniversary, future growth opportunities News Videos Rivian founder and CEO RJ Scaringe acknowledges that not everything has gone to plan amid supply chain shortages, geopolitical tensions and slower-than-expected consumer EV adoption , but he said he believes the next year will prove to be a catalyst for the company and investors. "2027 is really an inflection year for us," Scaringe told CNBC during an exclusive interview. "I'm excited to start to really show what we believe so fully, the potential of the business." R2 SUV Scaringe's bullishness comes as Rivian ramps up production of its midsize R2 SUV — meant to expand the brand to the mainstream market — and as the company continues to invest in its next generation of vehicle software and autonomy. Scaringe said the R2, with an entry-level model at about $45,000, remains the core business to be able to showcase its newest technologies. Rivian delivered a record 19,248 vehicles in the third quarter of 2026, up 46% year over year, and said R2 was already its best-selling vehicle by volume, outselling both its R1 flagship products and its commercial van. "That's going to define the business. The path to profitability, the path to very significant growth in revenue is all built around R2, and then some of the variants that come following R2," Scaringe said. Exterior of Rivian's new all-electric R2 SUV. Michael Wayland / CNBC For the most recent period, Rivian said the automotive cost of goods sold per vehicle improved by more than $12,000 quarter over quarter, helped by a higher R2 mix and better fixed-cost leverage. Rivian also is in the midst of building a new multibillion-dollar Georgia factory that Scaringe has said is necessary to get the company to the volumes it needs to achieve net profitability. Its sole factory in Normal, Illinois, is capable of producing 215,000 vehicles annually. That includes up to 155,000 R2s alongside R1 models and electric vans. Rivian said the Georgia plant will be capable of producing up to 300,000 units annually once the initial phase construction is completed in late 2028. Of course, all of that means additional capital spending and pressure on the company to improve profits. "We've made the decision to simultaneously work towards profitability … and deeply invest in our technology, and in particular in autonomy," Scaringe said. Profitability vs. cash burn Rivian's operating performance is improving, but several Wall Street analysts expect the company's investment requirements to rise significantly in 2027. Rivian generated $176 million of consolidated gross profit in the third quarter, but its automotive business posted an $80 million gross loss, while its software and services unit generated $256 million of gross profit at a 42% margin. Rivian's stock since going public on Nov. 10, 2021. Wall Street analysts broadly agree Rivian's R2 launch is showing encouraging early demand and lowering manufacturing costs, but they're concerned about whether that can offset rising autonomy spending, the Georgia factory buildout and continued cash burn. "Funding has long been a key debate for Rivian investors," Deutsche Bank analyst Edison Yu said in an Oct. 30 investor note after the company reported quarterly results that exceeded Wall Street's expectations . "The notion of a multi-year (even if credible) path to cash flow breakeven will be less attractive to investors." Rivian said during its late October earnings call that its total available future liquidity is expected to be about $13 billion when factoring in available credit and money from partnerships with Volkswagen and Uber as well as a $4.5 billion U.S. Department of Energy loan for the Georgia plant. Rivian said its cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments balance was $5.5 billion to end the third quarter. The company may still need to raise more capital. Scaringe said Rivian plans to be "opportunistic" about any additional capital raises, which have previously included equity deals with Volkswagen and Uber. "As we think about the environment looking out, we want to continue to position ourselves to be in a place to invest in the technology. And so that means we'll be opportunistic as it pertains to capital. But I want to be clear: We're like very focused on getting the profitability," Scaringe said. Autonomy The company has significantly upgraded the software capabilities and hardware on its vehicles to prepare them for autonomy technologies, or physical artificial intelligence, as Scaringe calls it. The next step in that is releasing "point-to-point" driving capabilities, in which the vehicles can drive on their own from destination to destination with the driver acting as a monitor in case of any unexpected problems. A motherboard from one of Rivian's all-electric vehicles. Michael Wayland / CNBC U.S. EV leader Tesla is the only automaker to currently offer those features on its vehicles. Scaringe said Rivian plans to not only catch up to Tesla's capabilities but exceed them as it uses multiple sensor types to allow the vehicle to "see" better, especially in inclement weather. "That's not like the finish line. ... Think of it as like the starting point where you suddenly have a more apples to apples comparison between Rivian and Tesla," Scaringe said. The release of point-to-point over the coming weeks and months, first to employees and then to customers, is expected to be followed by autonomous vehicles with Uber by 2028. Scaringe said he believes such technologies will become a differentiator for the company in the coming years. "I think it will go from a purchase consideration for maybe 10% of the buying public that's in the top five things considered in making a purchase decision to the No. 1 or No. 2 purchase consideration for the vast majority of buyers," Scaringe said.
